title: Billy — 18mo pygmy wether: straining with a swollen prepuce
presentation: 18-month-old castrated pygmy goat, straining and vocalising since yesterday, tail flagging, dribbling small amounts of blood-tinged urine. Fed a grain-based pellet ad libitum since weaning and castrated at two weeks old.

stages.title: Recognise the obstruction
stages.briefing: Depressed, grinding teeth, standing with a hunched back and stretched stance. HR 96 bpm, RR 36/min, temperature 38.2°C. Prepuce swollen and pulsating on palpation, crystals on the preputial hair. Bladder palpable and turgid on abdominal palpation. Rumen contractions reduced. Castrated at two weeks; diet high-grain, low-calcium.
stages.prompt: Which findings tell you this is obstructive rather than infectious?

options.label: Turgid, palpable bladder with a stretched stance
options.detail: Urine that cannot get out

options.label: Pulsating prepuce with crystals on the hair
options.detail: Obstruction at the urethral process

options.label: Early castration on a high-grain, low-calcium diet
options.detail: The two risk factors for caprine urolithiasis

options.label: Teeth grinding and depression
options.detail: Pain, from any cause

options.label: Temperature 38.2°C
options.detail: Normal, and it does not distinguish the two

stages.explanation: A turgid bladder and a stretched stance in a wether is a surgical clock starting: the pressure damages kidney and bladder wall within hours. Early castration leaves a narrow urethra and a grain ration inverts the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio, so the risk factors are in the history before you touch the goat. Pain and a normal temperature tell you nothing about the cause.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: The goat is bright enough to stand. You have blood tubes, ultrasound and radiography available, and surgery is an option.
stages.prompt: Which tests do you run before anaesthesia?

options.label: Serum potassium and sodium
options.detail: Hyperkalaemia is what stops the heart under anaesthesia

options.label: Urea and creatinine
options.detail: Grades the post-renal azotaemia

options.label: Blood gas or total carbon dioxide for acid-base status
options.detail: Metabolic acidosis needs correcting first

options.label: Abdominal and perineal ultrasound
options.detail: Bladder integrity, free fluid, hydronephrosis

options.label: Radiography of the urethra and bladder
options.detail: Locates and counts the calculi

options.label: Urine culture as the first priority
options.detail: Useful later; it does not change the next hour

options.label: Faecal egg count
options.detail: Irrelevant to an obstructed urethra

stages.explanation: The tests before anaesthesia are the ones that keep the goat alive through it: potassium, azotaemia and acid-base status decide whether you induce now or spend two hours correcting first. Imaging then tells you what operation you are doing. Culture is a reasonable afterthought and the wrong first move.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L (ref 3.5–5.5), sodium 138 mmol/L, chloride 98 mmol/L. Urea 34 mmol/L (ref 3.5–9.0), creatinine 620 µmol/L (ref 60–130). Total CO₂ 14 mmol/L (metabolic acidosis). Ultrasound: distended bladder with a thickened wall, bilateral mild hydronephrosis, no free abdominal fluid. Radiography: multiple small calculi in the urethra with the largest at the sigmoid flexure. Urinalysis from dribbled urine: pH 8.0, struvite crystals, blood 3+.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Complete or near-complete urethral obstruction with post-renal azotaemia
options.detail: Urea 34 mmol/L with a distended bladder

options.label: Life-threatening hyperkalaemia that must be treated before anaesthesia
options.detail: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L

options.label: Struvite calculi consistent with the grain-based diet
options.detail: Alkaline urine with struvite crystals

options.label: The bladder has not ruptured
options.detail: No free abdominal fluid on ultrasound

options.label: Primary kidney disease is the cause of the azotaemia
options.detail: The azotaemia is post-renal, from obstruction

options.label: Pyelonephritis is the leading diagnosis
options.detail: No fever, and the obstruction explains everything

stages.explanation: The hierarchy of these results is the lesson: the potassium is what kills in the next hour, the azotaemia is what determines the prognosis, and the calculi are what you operate on. Confirming an intact bladder changes the surgery you plan. Reading the azotaemia as kidney disease rather than obstruction would send you down a medical route while the bladder is still under pressure.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L, urea 34 mmol/L, creatinine 620 µmol/L, metabolic acidosis, multiple urethral struvite calculi, intact distended bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis, early-castrated wether on a grain ration.

options.label: Obstructive struvite urolithiasis with post-renal azotaemia and hyperkalaemia
options.detail: Obstruction, its metabolic consequences, and the stone type

options.label: Ruptured bladder with uroperitoneum
options.detail: No free fluid on ultrasound

options.label: Acute kidney injury from a nephrotoxin
options.detail: Does not explain urethral calculi or a turgid bladder

options.label: Pyelonephritis
options.detail: No fever, and obstruction accounts for the findings

options.label: Balanoposthitis with dysuria
options.detail: A swollen prepuce is a consequence here, not the disease

stages.explanation: Every clause of the diagnosis maps onto an action: correct the potassium and acidosis, decompress the bladder, then a tube cystostomy or perineal urethrostomy depending on the calculus load — and afterwards, ammonium chloride with a forage-based, correctly balanced ration, plus advice to delay castration in the next kids. The stone type is what makes the dietary advice specific rather than generic.
